caseno: Death Reference No. 95 of 2015 with Criminal Appeal No. 9940, 10065 & 10534 of 2015 with Jail Appeal No. 249 & 250 of 2015.
lawyer:
Harunur Rashid, Deputy Attorney-General with Zahid Ahammad (Hero) and Md Shafiquzzaman (Rana) Assistant Attorney-Generals—For the State. (In reference and respondents in the appeals) 
AKM Faiz, Senior Advocate with Advocate Mohammad Bakir Uddin Bhuiyan—For Convict-Appellant Safar Ali. (In Criminal Appeal No. 9940 of 2015) 
Khandaker Mohammad Musfiqul Huda, Advocate—For Convict-appellants. (In Criminal Appeal No. 10065 of 2015) 
Mantu Chandra Ghosh, Advocate—For the Convict-appellants Amir Hossain and Mohar Chand. (In Criminal Appeal No.10534 of 2015 & Jail A No.249 and of 2015) 
Rowshan Ara Begum, Advocate appointed as a State Defence Lawyer—For condemned-prisoner Amir Hossain alias Khokon. (In Reference)
parties:
State ------ Petitioner
VS
Amir Hossain alias Khokon and another Condemned------ Prisoners
full_judgment:
10. Mr AKM Faiz, learned Senior Advocate appearing in Criminal Appeal No.9940 of 2015 submits that in the FIR appellant Safar was suspected only. No specific allegation was brought against him there. There is no eyewitness to the occurrence. His conviction is solely based on his confession and that of the confessions of other two co-accused Noor Alam and Monir. But Safar's confession is neither true nor voluntary. The Magistrate who recorded his confession and that of others was not examined as witness. The confessions of three convicts and the evidence of 10, PW 11 prove that all the confessions were recorded at the same time, which was improbable considering the length of each confession. If the Magistrate was examined on oath, the defence could have put her questions about the above fact. The Magistrate did not comply with the provision of sections 164 and 364 of the Code in recording the confessions. He refers to the case of Babul alias Abdul Majid Khan and others vs the State, 42 DLR (AD) 186 and submits that in view of the ratio of the aforesaid case, it would be injudicious to rely upon the confession of Safar without calling the Magistrate as witness. To accept a confession and to rely upon it, the Tribunal has to see not only the forms under sections 164 and 364 of the Code were complied with but the substance underneath the law was equally adhered to. By not examining the Magistrate, the prosecution definitely denied the appellants right to cross-examine her. Mr Faiz then submits that even the confession of Safar is considered as true and made voluntarily and taken as evidence, it does not disclose any offence against him. He did not take .part in committing rape, nor did he even actively participate in the offence of murder. He just pressed the legs of the victim at the order or request of others. In such a case, the appellant has suffered more than 11½ (post and pre trial) years in jail. In view of the above position, Safar is entitled to the benefit of doubt and would be acquitted of the charge levelled against him. 

 11. Mr Mantu Chandra Ghosh, learned Advocate for condemned-prisoners Amir Hossain alias Khokon in Jail Appeal No. 249 of 2015 and for Mohar Chand in Criminal Appeal No. 10534 of 2015 and Jail Appeal No.250 of 2015 submits that appellant Khokon was named in the FIR as suspected but appellant Mohar was not named there. In the FIR, allegation was brought against Khokon that he offered love to victim Tania or he had affair with her and he (the informant) collected the said information from PWs 2, 3 and the source was PW 5 Roksana. If the information of having love affair with Khokon is found to be correct in that case he may be held responsible. But here Roksana as PW .5 did not support the facts as stated in the FIR. She disowned the fact of love affair between Khokon and Tania and was declared hostile. He refers to the evidence of PWs 1, 2 and 3 to show that they came to learn about the fact of love affair from PW 5. Therefore, the allegation brought in the FIR against Khokon and evidence of PWs 1, 2 and 3 to that effect do not corroborate the evidence of PW 5. None of the witnesses deposed that they saw Khokon or Mohar to go to the place of occurrence. The basis of conviction of appellants Khokon and Mohar are the confessions made by three other co-accused. Mr Ghosh refers to the cases of the State and another vs Abdul Kader alias Mobile Kader and others, 67 DLR (AD) 6; the State vs Delwar Hossaia and 7 others, 64 DLR 356 and Abdus Salam Mollah vs the State, 20 BLT (AD) 14 and submits that a confession of a co-accused is a very weaker type of evidence. The confession of co-accused in the sense that it may be taken into consideration against them along with other evidence cannot be the sole basis of conviction. In this case, there is no corroboration or support of those confessions from other sources. There is no link as required by law, either direct or circumstantial to find them guilty of the" offence. In respect of non-examination of the recording Magistrate, he adopts the submission made by Mr Faiz. Since the prosecution failed to prove the charge against his appellants by cogent and legal evidence, they are entitled to the acquittal. 

 13. Mr Huda then submits that convict Monir retracted the said confession, but the prosecution did not disprove the said fact alleged in the retraction petition as required under section 111 of the Evidence Act. He refers to the case of State represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Noagaon vs Md Palash, 20 BLC (AD) 348 and submits that in the absence of any reason for not calling the vital witness a negative inference against the prosecution may rightly be drawn. It is the burden of the prosecution to prove that the confessions were true and made voluntarily and it was duly taken, but here it hopelessly failed to prove it. Section 80 of the Evidence Act does not make the confession as substantive evidence. The confessions of his appellants shows that the part of committing rape so far it relates to them is exculpatory but other part of committing the crime of murder is inculpatory. The Court cannot accept the inculpatory part rejecting its exculpatory part. He refers to the case of the State vs Lalu Miah and another, 39 DLR (AD) 117 and submits that the appellants denied their participation of murder by showing utter involuntariness and attending coercion and adverse circumstances rendering the confessions exculpatory in nature, and, as such, the judgment and order of conviction basing on those cannot be sustained in law. The learned Judge could have used the confessions by declaring a co-accused as approver. But the Tribunal most erroneously relied on the confession of a co-accused against another accused. Mr Huda finally takes us through the confessions of Noor Alam and Monir and their examination under section 342 of the Code and submits that at the time of framing charge their ages were less than 16 years for which they could have been tried in Juvenile Court under the provisions of Children Act, 1974. Both the appellants have suffered in jail for more than 11½ years (post and pre trial). The prosecution failed to bring home the charge against the appellants beyond any shadow of doubt, and, as such, they should be acquitted. 

 15. In reply to the above submissions, the learned Deputy Attorney-General submits that the prosecution has been able to prove the time, place and manner of occurrence. The time as stated in the FIR has been proved by the witnesses. The place was the cremation centre near river as shown in the sketch-map and the manner of occurrence was rape followed by murder. The rape and murder have been proved by the inquest and the post-mortem examination reports. The FIR, sketch-map, evidence of PW 1, the autopsy and inquest reports are the substantive pieces of evidence which prove that the victim was raped and mudered in the place of occurrence and, thereafter, her body was thrown into the ditch. The above fact and evidence has been corroborated by the confessions of Safar, Monir and Noor Alam. Before lodgment of the FIR, police arrested some accused on the secret information. It was a circumstance for linking up the accused with the alleged offence. PWs 1, 2 and 3 stated the fact that Khokon had a love affair with the victim. They received the said information from PW 5 Roksana, but she was declared hostile. If the evidence of PWs 5-8 and 9 is considered altogether, it is found that they knew the fact of love affair between Khokon and victim Tania. But due to certain reason they could not lead evidence to that effect. He refers to the case of Siddique Munshi vs the State, 44 DLR (AD) 169 and submits that evidence of a hostile witness should not be rejected outright because he was declared hostile. Evidence of such witness sometimes reveals the truth. If corroboration is found from other sources there could be no reason to disbelieve his evidence and reject it outright. In the instant case, although the vital witnesses PWs 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9 were declared hostile but on analysis of their evidence it is found that they suppressed the fact and reveals that victim had a relation with Khokon. Regarding retraction of the confessions of Safar Ali and Monir Hossain, Mr Rashid submits that during their examination under section 342 of the Code all incriminating evidence including confessions were brought before them but the)., did not make any allegation of torture and ill treatment. Since, the witnesses were examined in their presence, they could have told it during their examination under section 342 of the Code. He refers to the case of Khalil Mia vs the State, 4 BLC (AD) 223 and submits that there the confession was specifically brought to the notice of the condemned-prisoner while examining him under section 342 of the Code but he did not complain regarding the nature of confession. The confession was believed to be true and voluntary and conviction was maintained. 

 16. He then submits that the prosecution took their best effort to examine Magistrate Momana Khatun, who recorded confessions, but her attendance could not be ensured. He refers to an order of the Tribunal and submits that the High Court Division passed an order to dispose of the case expeditiously and, as such, the prosecution failed to examine the Magistrate. The Tribunal concluded examination of prosecution witnesses on an application of the learned Public Prosecutor (PP) and then examined the accused under section 342 of the Code. Under the circumstances, the confession of the accused is permitted by law to take into evidence under section 80 of the Evidence Act. He refers to the cases of State vs Munir and another, 1 BLC 345; Abul Khayer and 3 others vs the State, 46 DLR 212 and the State vs Tajul Islam and 8 others, 48 DLR 305 and submits that in the case in hand the Tribunal rightly considered the confessions of Safar, Monir and Noor Alam as evidence under section 80 of the Evidence Act. He then refers to the case of Md Moinul Haque and another vs the State, 56 DLR (AD) 81 and submits that under section 32 of the Penal Code, acts means omission and, as such, those accused who did not commit rape but were present in the place of occurrence and took part in the commission of murder should be held responsible for the offence under section 6(4) of the Act. He adds that under section 30 of the Evidence Act, a confession of a co-accused may be used against other accused for the same offence in a joint trial. Here, the inquest, postmortem report, evidence of doctor and IO support it and the circumstance corroborate the confessions of three accused, and, as such, the Tribunal rightly passed conviction and sentence against the convicts under section 6(4) of the Ain, 1995. The reference thus would be accepted and the appeals be dismissed. 

 41. Since the prosecution had taken its effort best to examine the Magistrate but failed, we find that the Tribunal correctly took the confessions for consideration. The case reported in 42 DLR (AD) 186, referred to by Mr Faiz do not apply here because there the Magistrate was not at all called for to depose as witness. In this case, learned PP although did not file any application in the Tribunal to admit the confessions into evidence by marking it but the learned Judge has taken it for consideration under section 80 of the Evidence Act. We find no harm in doing so. In Sharmin Rima's Case (1 BLC 345), in Nidarhbad murder case (48 DLR 305) and in Abut Khayer's case (46 DLR 212) this Division found no necessity of formal proof of a confession duly recorded by a Magistrate in accordence with the provisions of section 164 of the Code. In such a case, the examination of the recording Magistrate is not imperative. The judgment of the abovecited cases have been affirmed by our Appellate Division. However, in this case the Court is to determine whether the confessions are true and made voluntarily before relying on those. 

 42. It transpires that in the FIR, informant suspected only convict Amir Hossain alias Khokon and Safar as offenders. The basis of suspicion was the information supplied by PW 5 Roksana, a friend of Tania. From the evidence of PWs 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9, we find that they did not support the prosecution case that Tania had any love affair with convict Khokon. From the cross-examination of the prosecution to them, we find that PW 5 knew the fact of love affair between Khokon and Tania. It seems that the accused and the above witnesses were from the same locality for which they did not dare to depose supporting the fact in toto. But PW 5 admitted that police recorded her statement. She heard that Tania was murdered after being raped, but she could not remember the names of the accused. In the case reported in 44 DLR (AD) 169, it has been held that the evidence of hostile witnesses should not be thrown outright. Their 'evidence should be considered cautiously as a whole and if found corroborated from other sources, it can be relied upon. Here, although the hostile witnesses did not support the prosecution case fully but for that reason only their evidence should not be rejected in limine. On close scrutiny of their evidence, we find that Khokan had an affair with Tania but they have attempted to suppress it in evidence. 

 51. In view of the above position, we find that prosecution has been able to prove the charge against condemned-prisoners Amir Hossain alias Khokon, Mohar Chand and convict Safar Ali beyond any reasonable doubt. We find no relevency of the cases cited by the lerned Advocates for the appellants in this case. We further do not find the principle of Yesmin murder case [56 DLR (AD) 81], as referred by the learned Deputy Attorney-General befitting here to maintain conviction of Monir and Noor Alam. 

 52. The sentence of death inflicted upon non confessing convicts Amir Hossain alias Khokon and Mohar Chand is justified, because the offence is heinous in nature and both of them committed rape upon the victim and, thereafter, murdered her by taking active participation. Both of them were masterminds. Although, as per the confessions Tania and Khokon were consenting parties, but Tania was a girl of 14 (fourteen) years according to the FIR and evidence. The age of the victim was not challenged by the defence. Tania's consent, if any, was no consent in the eye of law. Khokon, as lover of Tania, could have resisted the other convicts (Mohar, Taru and Safar) but he did not do it. He took the vital role in committing the murder. Now a days, the people are losing their faith in dispensation of criminal justice by the Court for the reason that they either acquit the accused on technical grounds or take a lenient view in awarding sentence. Judges are sons of this soil. They are duty bound and worth to the family members of the victim as well as to the society. It is the high time that the Court should realise that they have duty to the legal heirs and relations of the victim and also to the society. Sentence as awarded should be such, which should act as a deterrent to the commission of offences. In the case of Md Shukur Ali and others vs the State, 74 DLR (AD) 11 our Apex Court confirmed the death sentence of non confessing accused in view of the consistency of the confessions made by other co-accused implicating the main accused of the offence. Convict Khokon and. Mohar, although were of tender age but they committed the offence like grown up men and professional killers. We find no reason to commute their sentence of death considering their culpability of offence.
